title: Logger core in Java
idea: The core logger is one `log` method: check the level, build one LogRecord with an injected clock, then hand it to every appender, isolating each failure.

analogy.text: A newsroom wire. An editor drops minor stories, stamps the rest with the time, and copies each to every subscribing paper. One paper's broken press does not stop the others.
analogy.breaks: Papers reprint at leisure; a FileAppender writes during the call.

points: The level check runs first, before the message string is even built.
A `Supplier` message defers costly string building until the level passes.
`Clock` and the thread name are captured once, into the record.
A failing appender is counted and skipped; the caller never sees the exception.

hero.title: One log call through the core

steps.caption: The service calls `debug` with a lambda. No string exists yet.
DEBUG is below INFO. The call returns at once and the lambda never runs.
Next the service calls `error` for payment OD-1.
ERROR passes the check. Now the lambda runs and builds the message.
One immutable record captures level, message, clock time and thread name.
Each appender gets the same record. The broken one throws; the logger counts it and moves on.
Console and file still write the line. ERROR flushes the file buffer at once.
Control returns to the service with no exception, whatever the appenders did.

code.title: Logger, appenders, formatter
code.caption: The complete core: lazy messages, an injected clock, console and file appenders, and failure isolation. The temp file path is never printed.

walk.text: A fixed clock, a temp log file and one shared pattern formatter.
Three appenders, one broken on purpose. try-with-resources closes the file.
DEBUG is never built; INFO and ERROR are written, and the broken appender fails both.
The formatter pads the level, so columns line up.
Buffered file writes, flushed on ERROR so important lines reach the OS at once (flush is not fsync).
A `volatile` threshold, changed by `setLevel`, is seen at once by every logging thread.
The algorithm: filter, build one record, fan out, swallow and count failures.

code.title: Inherited levels
code.caption: A LogManager hands out one Logger per name and now owns the levels. A logger without its own level inherits from the nearest dotted parent.

walk.text: Root is WARN; `app` and `app.db` get their own levels.
Ask three loggers for their effective level and whether DEBUG is on.
The same name returns the same Logger; a parent change reaches it.
`computeIfAbsent` creates each named Logger exactly once.
Strip the last segment until a configured level or the root is found.
The Logger asks the manager each time, so level changes apply at once.

pitfalls: Never build log strings before the level check; use a `Supplier` or placeholders.
Do not let an appender's IOException escape into the business call.
Do not call `Instant.now()` in the logger; inject a `Clock` for repeatable tests.

quiz.q: What does CoreLogger print for failed appends?
quiz.why: DEBUG stops at the level check. INFO and ERROR each reach BrokenAppender, which throws. The logger counts both and moves on.

takeaway: Filter first, build one record, fan out, and never throw into callers.

starters: Why flush only on ERROR instead of after every line?
Should the failed-append count be exposed as a metric?
How does the effective-level walk compare to caching levels per logger?
